title: India Sugar Prices Hit Record High on Tight Supplies and Festival Demand
excerpt: Wholesale prices have surged 10% in a month, with inventories heading for their lowest level in over three decades. The rally is expected to persist through November as festival season consumption peaks.
body:
• Indian wholesale sugar prices have jumped 10% in the past month to a record ₹4,716 per 100 kg in Kolhapur, a key trading hub.
  • Mill inventories at the start of the new season in October are expected to fall to about 3.5 million tons — the lowest level in more than 30 years.
  • The government banned sugar exports and imposed stock limits last month, but prices continue to climb ahead of the festival season.
  • Sugar stocks including Balrampur Chini, Dwarikesh Sugar and Shree Renuka Sugars are expected to benefit from improved producer margins.

Indian sugar prices have surged to record highs, jumping 10 percent over the past month as tightening supplies collide with the onset of the country's peak festival demand season, traders and industry officials told Reuters.

Wholesale sugar prices in Kolhapur — a key trading hub in the western state of Maharashtra, India's largest sugar-producing region — have climbed to ₹4,716 per 100 kg, a level not previously reached. The rally is expected to persist for at least the next three months.

Festival Season Fuels Demand

India's sugar consumption typically rises sharply from August through November as the country celebrates major festivals including Ganesh Chaturthi, Dussehra and Diwali. Traditional sweets and confectionery — staples of festival celebrations — drive a seasonal spike in demand that mills are struggling to meet this year.

"Demand has picked up ahead of the festival season, but mills are holding back supplies and releasing stocks gradually, expecting prices to climb further."

— Ashok Jain, President, Bombay Sugar Merchants Association

The supply squeeze is acute. Production in the current season has fallen short of annual consumption, and mills exported about 800,000 tons of sugar before the government stepped in. Inventories held by mills at the start of the new season on October 1 are expected to drop to approximately 3.5 million tons — the lowest level in more than three decades.

Government Scrambles to Contain Prices

New Delhi has already moved aggressively to cool the market. Last month, the government banned sugar exports outright until September 30, 2026, and imposed stock limits on mills and traders. The export ban — shifting sugar's status from "restricted" to "prohibited" — came after revised production estimates showed output falling below domestic demand for a second consecutive year.

Despite these measures, prices have continued to climb. The rally adds to inflationary pressures that are already testing policymaker patience: retail inflation breached the Reserve Bank of India's target for the first time in 17 months in June.

Supplies Won't Ease Until November

Relief is unlikely before November, when mills begin crushing the new-season sugarcane crop. Until then, the market must rely entirely on the current season's production, which has proven insufficient.

Weather risks compound the problem. Concerns about El Niño conditions disrupting the monsoon have raised the possibility that next season's output could also fall below initial estimates. Thailand, the world's second-largest exporter, is also expected to see production decline as farmers shift to cassava due to low cane prices.

Producer Stocks to Watch

The sustained price rally is expected to boost margins for sugar producers. Shares of Balrampur Chini, Dwarikesh Sugar, Shree Renuka Sugars and Dalmia Bharat Sugar are positioned to benefit, dealers said, as higher realisation prices flow through to earnings over the coming quarters.

For Indian households — including those in the diaspora who send money home for festival preparations — the price surge means higher costs for the mithai and sweets that are central to celebrations from Kolkata's Durga Puja to Mumbai's Ganesh festival.
